opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that you should think of it the way you'd think about diversifying a portfolio. I wouldn't ask, "What's the best country?" I'd ask, "How do I make sure no single country can break me?" Because history shows us that countries rise and decline in big cycles, and the conditions that seem permanent at any moment usually aren't.

So I'd look at a handful of measurable things. Is the country financially healthy, or does it have a lot of debt and is it printing money to pay for it? Is there internal order, or is there a lot of conflict between left and right, rich and poor? Is it at risk of being pulled into a major external conflict? Does it have strong education, innovation, and a culture of hard work and civility? And is there rule of law, so that if you build something, it stays yours? You want places where people treat each other well and where capital and talent want to come, rather than leave.

Then I'd structure the business accordingly. Keep your people, your intellectual property, your banking, and your legal entities spread across a few well-chosen jurisdictions, so that if one of them changes its rules, imposes capital controls, or gets caught up in a conflict, you can keep operating. Hold your wealth in more than one currency, too. And stay mobile. Design things so that you can move before you have to, because when conditions get bad, the doors tend to close, and by then it's too late.

The places that do well tend to be the neutral, well-run ones that get along with the different sides, the ones that stay out of the fights. So my principle is this: know the indicators, watch them, don't fall in love with any one place, and never let a single point of failure be able to take you out. Diversifying well is the most important thing you can do, in investing and in building a business.

r001.rationale: It mentions education and innovation as factors for assessing countries, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends spreading people, intellectual property, banking, and legal entities across several jurisdictions.

r003.rationale: It explains that countries rise and decline in cycles and that conditions that seem permanent may change, so a favored location may not remain favorable.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that you're asking the right question, because most people don't ask it. Most people build where they happened to be born, and that's an accident, not a decision. Where you locate yourself is one of the biggest bets you'll ever make, and you should treat it like one.

So here's how I think about it. I look at countries the way I look at any investment, which means I look at the fundamentals and I look at where they're headed, not where they are today. There are a handful of things I'd measure. First, is the place financially sound? Does it have more income than expenses, more assets than liabilities, or is it borrowing to live beyond its means? Second, is there internal order? Are people fighting with each other over wealth and values in a way that's getting worse, or is there a sense of shared rules that people respect? Third, is there rule of law, meaning if I build something, can someone take it from me arbitrarily? And fourth, do they value education, innovation and hard work, because that's what produces the next generation of talent I'd be hiring.

Then there's the external dimension. Is this country in a rising position in the world order or a declining one, and is it likely to get pulled into conflict? Because a great business in the wrong place at the wrong time still loses.

Now, to the heart of your question, not tying yourself to one country. That's really about diversification, and it's the same principle I've used my whole life. You don't know the future, so you don't want to be dependent on one outcome. So I'd structure things so the business can operate from more than one place. Have your legal entity, your capital, your people and your markets not all concentrated in a single jurisdiction. Keep some assets where they'd be safe if things went badly where you live. Build relationships in several countries so that if one door closes, you can walk through another. That's not disloyalty, it's prudence.

And I'd add one more thing, because people get this wrong. They think about where the taxes are lowest. Taxes are one input, but they're not the thing that kills you. What kills you is being somewhere when the rules of the game change on you, whether that's capital controls, expropriation, civil disorder or war. History shows that happens far more often than people expect, and it tends to happen when debt is high, wealth gaps are large and a rising power is challenging an existing one. We're in that kind of period now.

So practically, I'd pick a primary base that scores well on those fundamentals, I'd make sure it's a place I actually want to live and can attract great people to, and then I'd deliberately build optionality so that I'm never a hostage to any one government's decisions. Think of yourself as a global citizen with roots in a few good places, not a tenant of one landlord.

r001.rationale: It mentions education, innovation, and hiring talent, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends structuring the business to operate from more than one place and avoiding concentration of its people, capital, and markets in a single jurisdiction.

r003.rationale: It says to assess where countries are headed rather than where they are today, and notes that rules and country conditions can change, conveying that a location’s current advantages may not last.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate three decisions: where your customers are, where your people are, and where you put your capital. Those don’t necessarily have to be in the same country.

For each location, I’d ask: Is there respect for the rule of law? Can I find the talent I need? Are the finances sound? And if conditions change, can I move my money and continue operating?

Then I’d stress-test the business. What happens if taxes rise, capital movements are restricted, or two countries stop trading with each other? You don’t need to predict exactly what will happen. You need to avoid having one outcome determine whether you survive.

You’ll always have obligations wherever you operate. But you can build across countries so that you have alternatives. The objective is to benefit from what different places offer while keeping the flexibility to adapt.

r001.rationale: It asks whether the needed talent is available, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends building across countries so the business has alternatives and can adapt, communicating a presence in multiple geographic locations.

r003.rationale: It discusses changing conditions and flexibility, but does not clearly explain that a location best for the business now may not remain best over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking: what does the business need to succeed, and where are those conditions best? Where is the talent? Where are your customers? Is there respect for the rule of law? Can you move capital, and can you operate with confidence?

You don’t have to make all those decisions in one place. Where you live, where you incorporate, and where you hire can be different. But you have to understand the tax and legal obligations that come with that.

And then I’d think about diversification. If your customers, your money, and your operations are all dependent on one country, you have a concentration of risk. You can love a country and still diversify. The important thing is to preserve your ability to adapt as conditions change.

r001.rationale: It asks where the talent is, but does not specify concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends spreading where the business lives, incorporates, and hires across different places, and warns against depending on one country.

r003.rationale: It mentions adapting as conditions change, but does not explain that a location that is best now may not remain best over time.
